title: Ang 469–475: Asa di Var, second half
hook: sweetness, humility and the thread of compassion
tomorrow: who stretched the whole world out on a loom?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dawn ballad: a hundred moons, and still dark without a guide. The ballad's second half turns from light to a thread.
screen: `THE DAWN BALLAD.` → `FROM LIGHT TO A THREAD.`

segments.voice: Thread bracelets are everywhere: the band from summer camp, the string someone tied on a wrist, the one worn so long it's forgotten. Threads fray, though. They snap in the wash. On ang 471, Guru Nanak describes one that doesn't. In paraphrase: it doesn't break, doesn't get dirty, doesn't burn, doesn't get lost.
screen: `THE BRACELET YOU FORGET YOU WEAR.` → `THREADS FRAY AND SNAP.` → `ONE THAT DOESN'T.`

segments.voice: He spins it from virtues, in paraphrase: make compassion, daya, the cotton; contentment, santokh, the thread; self-control the knot; truth the twist. That's a thread for the soul, and whoever wears it is blessed. A page earlier, on ang 470, the same Asa di Var names what holds every good quality together: sweetness and humility, Nanak, are the essence. So, today's question: what's worth wearing? Here's how a neighbor tradition answers. In the Hebrew Bible, the prophet Micah asks what the LORD requires, and answers, in the 1917 Jewish translation: “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God.” Mercy and humility, in Micah's words; compassion and humility, in Guru Nanak's. That's real common ground. And an honest difference. Micah speaks as a prophet of Israel's God and names what is required: a command, in the covenant language of his people. Guru Nanak gives a picture instead: something you spin from your own virtues and wear, a thread for any soul. One is a requirement, one is a garment. Both ask for mercy and a low, sweet heart.
screen: `COMPASSION IS THE COTTON.` · `SWEETNESS AND HUMILITY: THE ESSENCE.` · `MICAH: LOVE MERCY, WALK HUMBLY.` · `A REQUIREMENT, AND A GARMENT.` · then, large: `THE THREAD.`

segments.voice: Read ang 470 first if you can. If something sweet is nearby, a raisin, a bit of honey, a sip of chai, taste it slowly and let the sweetness last. If not, hold a piece of thread or string and run it through your fingers, and rest with one word: sweetness.
Ang 469. The page where the second half of Asa di Var carries on, toward the thread of compassion.
Worth keeping: the thread, spun from compassion and worn on the inside. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The second half of Asa di Var is sung at the morning kirtan in gurdwaras and read in order in Raag Asa; the saloks on sweetness and humility and on the thread of compassion are among its lines Sikhs return to.

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 written: shape wisdom. The unity thread: one question (what's worth wearing?), the Sikh answer (a thread spun from compassion, contentment, self-control and truth; sweetness and humility the essence), a neighbor tradition in its own words and source (Micah 6:8, JPS 1917, quoted exactly for the clause used), and one honest difference (Micah names what the LORD requires, as a prophet of Israel's God; Guru Nanak gives a picture of a garment). No ranking; neither called the same.

Micah 6:8 JPS 1917: the clause 'to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God' is quoted; the full verse in JPS 1917 begins 'It hath been told thee, O man, what is good'. Confirm exact wording. A Jewish reviewer may want to confirm the 'covenant language' framing.

Ang 471 janeu salok paraphrased (compassion the cotton, contentment the thread, continence/self-control the knot, truth the twist; it doesn't break, get soiled, burn or get lost). The salok's setting (Guru Nanak declining the sacred thread at his own ceremony, addressing the pandit) is deliberately not told, so no tradition is made a foil. Keeper to confirm this choice and the Ang.
